findings.title: Pin and verify the remotely executed installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build downloads and executes whatever content https://example.com/install.sh serves at that moment. A changed or compromised installer can run arbitrary commands during the build and persist them in the produced image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remotely executed installer
findings.whyItBreaks: This newly added line downloads mutable content at build time and pipes it directly to sh. A compromised or changed endpoint makes image builds execute attacker-controlled commands without version or checksum verification.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes the current response from https://example.com/install.sh. A compromised origin or an upstream script change can execute arbitrary code during the build and produce a compromised image.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported wrapper ignores Load's ErrMissing and returns "", making an absent key indistinguishable from a present key with an empty value.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key failures instead of returning an empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported API discards Load's ErrMissing and returns "", which is also a valid stored map value. Consumers cannot distinguish absence from an intentionally empty value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key status in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported function ignores Load's ErrMissing and returns "", which is also a valid map value. Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a stored empty value.

findings.title: Keep result sends within Run's lifetime
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation returned only after every result was sent. The new goroutines allow Run to return while sends are pending; a caller that closes results after Run returns will panic with "send on closed channel".

findings.title: Wait for worker sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed goroutines outlive Run, whereas the prior loop completed every send before returning. A caller can reasonably use Run's return as completion and close its provided results channel, causing a later goroutine to panic; without a receiver, those goroutines can also remain blocked indefinitely.

findings.title: Wait for submitted jobs before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed loop starts one goroutine per job and then returns without waiting. If result consumption is slow or absent, each goroutine blocks on `results <- j * 2`, retaining an unbounded number of goroutines for a large jobs slice. This also newly permits Run to return with result sends still in flight.

findings.title: Require admin privileges before allowing record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: With `||`, a session where `isAdmin` is false but `tenantId` matches the record returns true, allowing any tenant member to delete records. It also allows an admin from a different tenant to delete the record.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant ownership for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || allows any non-admin user in the record's tenant to delete it, and allows an admin from a different tenant to delete it. The previous policy required both checks.

findings.title: Require administrator status and tenant match for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing && with || authorizes deletion when either condition holds: non-admin users in the record tenant and administrators from other tenants now pass, although both were previously denied.

findings.title: Propagate invalid-settings errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid stored settings formerly threw and prevented updateFontSize from calling save. They now become {theme:"light",fontSize:14}; updateFontSize then changes the font size and persists that fallback, silently replacing the user's prior theme/configuration.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before saving settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch converts malformed or schema-invalid settings to DEFAULTS. updateFontSize then changes fontSize and saves that fallback, so an invalid stored value such as a dark theme with an invalid fontSize is replaced with light-theme defaults instead of surfacing the parse failure.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch converts malformed or schema-invalid settings into defaults. updateFontSize then modifies those defaults and saves them, overwriting the original invalid data instead of preserving the prior parse/validation failure.

findings.title: Keep report artifacts aligned with builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed code labels the report with build.ref(branch) but fetches artifacts using build.ref("verified"). If those refs differ, consumers receive artifacts from a different commit than builtFrom identifies.

findings.title: Retrieve artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is resolved from the caller-provided `branch`, while `artifacts` are fetched from the separate `verified` ref. When those refs differ, the returned report associates artifacts with the wrong commit.

findings.title: Return artifacts for the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When branch resolves to a different commit than "verified", builtFrom contains the branch commit while artifacts contains files from the verified commit. Consumers receive a self-contradictory BuildReport and can publish or inspect artifacts for the wrong build.

findings.title: Restore limit enforcement for positive limits
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, recentEntries returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20 and writes every returned entry into its 20-slot array, extending it when there are more than 20 inputs.

findings.title: Restore the requested result limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function now returns all reversed entries instead of at most `limit`. `renderFeed` passes 20 and copies every returned entry, so inputs with more than 20 entries produce output longer than 20.

findings.title: Restore the limit slice
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns every entry rather than at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20, then writes the oversized result into its 20-entry page, extending the returned array beyond 20 when more entries exist.

findings.title: Keep entry-count equal to the emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are now removed from rendered rows, but the header still declares entries.length. Consumers validating the manifest's entry-count will receive a count larger than its record count.

findings.title: Keep entry-count aligned with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When an entry has stale=true, this new filter omits its row while the returned header still receives entries.length. The serialized manifest therefore declares more entries than it contains.

findings.title: Count only emitted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When an entry has stale=true, it is omitted from the rows but the # entry-count header still uses entries.length. The manifest therefore declares more entries than it contains.

findings.title: Preserve the FormatLegacyID exported API
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting the exported `ids.FormatLegacyID` function is a source-incompatible change: downstream modules that call it will no longer compile. Restore it or provide a deprecated compatibility wrapper.

findings.title: Restore the exported FormatLegacyID compatibility contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported FormatLegacyID symbol makes existing downstream consumers calling ids.FormatLegacyID fail to compile on upgrade. The deleted test demonstrates the previously supported formatting contract.

findings.title: Restore the removed shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes the exported `shippingQuote(order)` function. Consumers importing it from `src/orders` can no longer compile or load after upgrading, despite the calculation having moved to `quoteShipping`.

findings.title: Retain shippingQuote as a compatibility export
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed module no longer exports shippingQuote; consumers importing this public symbol will fail to compile or resolve it after upgrading.

score.error: critic produced no summary or checked list (likely malformed output)

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but this implementation unconditionally throws. Every caller now fails regardless of input instead of receiving the transformed string.

findings.title: Restore execute's string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported execute function declares a string return type, but the changed body unconditionally throws. Every consumer call now fails rather than receiving the prior uppercase result.

findings.title: Return the declared string result instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed body unconditionally throws, so every caller of the exported function receives an exception rather than its declared string result. The base implementation returned input.toUpperCase().

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only handling path
findings.whyItBreaks: The new viewer rejection at src/handler.ts:18 makes handle() return "rejected" for active viewers, so its existing viewer branch at src/handler.ts:24 can no longer return "read-only".

findings.title: Preserve viewer read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: The new viewer guard returns false for active viewers, so handle() returns "rejected" before reaching its viewer-specific "read-only" branch.

findings.title: Allow eligible viewers to reach the read-only handler
findings.whyItBreaks: The new role check rejects active viewers before handle can reach its existing viewer branch, so requests that previously returned "read-only" now return "rejected".

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts savable
findings.whyItBreaks: The added payment condition is shared by submitOrder and saveDraft. For a draft with payment="missing", canProceed now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked"; before this change it returned "saved".

findings.title: Keep draft saves independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: The added payment predicate makes canProceed return false for a draft with payment="missing". saveDraft uses this shared predicate and now returns "blocked", preventing users from saving an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep snapshot files aligned with its commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested channel head differs from "stable", the returned Snapshot exposes the channel head in `commit` but obtains `files` from stable. Consumers cannot reliably use the reported commit to identify the returned files.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any requested channel whose head differs from `stable`, the returned `Snapshot.commit` is that channel's head while `Snapshot.files` are read from `stable`. Consumers can therefore publish or inspect file contents that do not belong to the commit the snapshot identifies.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, the returned Snapshot reports that channel's commit but contains `stable`'s file list. Consumers cannot reconstruct or publish the stated commit correctly.

findings.title: Honor the advertised limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling build("item", 1) still returns 10 items because the implementation always assigns max_count = 10 and never reads limit. The new parameter therefore promises observable output capping that the function does not provide.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=2)` still returns 10 entries because the body always assigns `max_count = 10`; the new parameter promises an observable result cap but does not affect output.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly introduced name promises a positive integer, but the changed function still returns `int(value)`, accepting 0 and negatives. `charge("-1")` consequently returns -100.

findings.title: Validate positivity promised by parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int returns zero and negative integers despite its new positive-integer contract; charge immediately consumes that result and emits zero or negative cent amounts.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negative values. charge() relies on this parser before multiplying, so charge("-1") returns -100 rather than rejecting an invalid amount.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame instead of mutating it
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values copied df and returned the modified copy. The new assignment writes directly into df, so callers that retain or reuse their input unexpectedly observe its value column changed.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function made a copy and updated that copy; it now writes through df.loc and returns the same object. Any caller that retains df for later use will observe its original values overwritten after calling apply_values.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame when applying mappings
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation transformed a copy and returned it. This change writes through to df, so callers that retain and reuse the input DataFrame will observe its value column unexpectedly modified.

findings.title: Reject non-positive inputs in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly renamed public function promises a positive integer, but "-7" parses successfully and returns -7. Its in-file consumer, charge at src/parse.rs:6, therefore returns -700.

findings.title: Reject non-positive input before returning it
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1` and `parse_positive_int("0")` returns `0`, despite its public name promising a positive result. Its caller then turns `-1` into a negative charge (`-100`).

findings.title: Reject non-positive integers in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int("-5") returns -5 because it directly parses a signed i64. Its new public name promises a positive value, while the in-file consumer charge returns -500 for that input.

findings.title: Avoid moving items before computing its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` moves and discards the `Vec`; the subsequent `items.len()` borrows a moved value, causing compilation to fail.

findings.title: Borrow items in the debug statement
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns the `Vec<String>` by value; as a discarded statement it moves and drops `items`. The subsequent `items.len()` therefore fails with use-after-move error E0382.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the replay revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` is resolved from `pinnedTag`, but `changedPaths` is computed from `latest`. The public `Changeset` contract says consumers replay on `fromRevision`, so a pinned revision behind `latest` receives paths derived from the wrong revision.

findings.title: Derive changed paths from the reported base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision remains the resolved pinned tag, but changedPaths is now read using the unrelated latest revision. Consumers replay these paths on fromRevision, so a pinned tag behind latest yields a changeset whose paths do not correspond to its declared base.

findings.title: Compute paths against the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract says changedPaths are computed against and replayed on fromRevision. This changed code returns the revision for pinnedTag but computes paths from the distinct latest revision. When pinnedTag is not latest, consumers receive paths paired with the wrong base revision.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration runs, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`, which fails with an unknown-column error.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`, which will fail with an undefined-column error.

findings.title: Update queries before renaming the email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; deployments that apply the migration will fail that query.

findings.title: Remove the hard-coded live billing API key
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line commits a `bk_live_` credential into repository history, exposing it to every clone and artifact while removing deploy-time secret configuration.

findings.title: Restore environment-sourced billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: This commits a bk_live credential into source control and makes every deployment use that one billing account, ignoring each environment's BILLING_API_KEY. The key is exposed to every repository reader and cannot be rotated or tenant-scoped through deployment configuration.

findings.title: Remove and rotate the committed billing API key
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient now returns a hard-coded bk_live credential to every caller. The secret is exposed in repository history and cannot be rotated or scoped per deployment; the prior missing-secret failure is also bypassed.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization check
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard returns "forbidden" for admins, while non-admins with archived projects reach `db.delete(project.id)`. This reverses the prior authorization behavior and permits unauthorized destructive deletion.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization check
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed early return rejects admins, then permits any non-admin to delete an archived project, creating an authorization bypass and destructive unauthorized write.

findings.title: Require admin authorization before deleting a project
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard returns "forbidden" for admins, but an archived project supplied by a non-admin reaches db.delete at line 14. This reverses authorization for a destructive operation.

findings.title: Restore defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist, but startup now immediately subscripts settings. A missing settings file, which previously started with one worker, now raises TypeError before startup can return.

findings.title: Restore defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings` returns `None` when `path` does not exist, but `startup` now immediately subscripts it. Starting without a settings file therefore raises `TypeError` rather than returning the prior default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Restore missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (app/config.py:6-7). The changed startup path then evaluates settings["workers"] (app/config.py:14), raising TypeError rather than returning the prior default of one worker.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed error branch logs a Gateway.Submit failure but then reaches `return nil`, causing the exported Charge API to report a failed payment as successful.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed error branch logs a Gateway.Submit failure and then reaches `return nil`. Callers of the exported Charge function therefore receive success when a gateway submission fails.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: On a Gateway.Submit error, exported Charge logs the failure then returns nil. Callers cannot distinguish a failed payment from a completed charge.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches `name`, a fetch for the same name under tenant B hits `settings:<name>` and returns tenant A's value without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, name)`. This can disclose tenant-scoped settings across tenants.

findings.title: Preserve the tenant-aware invalidate API
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function changed from `invalidate(tenantId, name)` to `invalidate(name)`. Existing JavaScript callers passing two arguments now delete `settings:<tenantId>` rather than the cached setting, leaving stale data; TypeScript callers fail type-checking.

findings.title: Keep tenant identity in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still fetches values using tenantId, but its cache key is now derived only from name. Once one tenant caches a name, a different tenant requesting that name receives the cached first tenant's value.

findings.title: Preserve the exported invalidate tenantId parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function changed from invalidate(tenantId, name) to invalidate(name). Existing TypeScript two-argument calls no longer type-check, while JavaScript calls with the former arguments delete settings:<tenantId> rather than the requested setting key.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: `settingsFor` fetches values by `(tenantId, name)`, but the changed key is based only on `name`. Once one tenant caches a setting, another tenant requesting that name receives the cached value before its tenant-scoped store is queried.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for each SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls can both read remaining=1 before either resumes after awaiting save. Both then set stock to 0 and resolve true, reserving the same unit twice.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations before persisting
findings.whyItBreaks: The new await occurs before the stock map is decremented. With stock=1, two overlapping calls can both read remaining=1, each save 0, then each set stock to 0 and return true—confirming two reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Preserve the public construction API
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported class previously supported `new Inventory()`, but the new required constructor parameter makes existing TypeScript consumers fail to type-check. JavaScript consumers can still omit it, leaving `store` undefined and causing stocked reservations to throw when calling `this.store.save`.

findings.title: Preserve the synchronous reserve contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `reserve` returned `false` immediately for unavailable stock. Existing callers such as `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` now receive a truthy Promise and proceed even when the eventual result is `false`.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await occurs after reading stock and before updating it. Two concurrent calls with one item remaining can each read `1`, each save `0`, and each resolve `true`, accepting two reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Remove the stale seconds-to-milliseconds conversion in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, while src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). The first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) rather than 1 second; capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (8h20m).

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 ms, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before sleeping. A first failed attempt therefore waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1 second; later attempts can wait 30,000,000 ms, effectively stalling retries.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff now returns milliseconds, but retry still multiplies the result by 1000. Its first failed attempt therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) rather than 1,000 ms.

findings.title: Return the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `defer f.Close()` discards Close's error. If Flush succeeds but Close reports a finalization failure, exported Save returns nil; before this change it returned the Close error.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed deferred Close discards its error. When Flush succeeds but Close fails, this exported function returns nil, whereas it previously returned the Close error.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `defer f.Close()` discards Close's return value. Previously, a successful Flush followed by a Close failure was returned by Save; now Save returns nil, allowing callers to treat a failed final write as persisted.

findings.title: Include the page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds are half-open [start, end), but range(start, end - 1) excludes index end - 1. One-row pages become empty and every page loses its last row; render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) emits incomplete output.

findings.title: Include the page’s final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed half-open bounds make end exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) also excludes end - 1. Each non-empty page window therefore loses its final row; render_page at lib/pagination.py:40 and summarize at lib/pagination.py:52 emit incomplete output.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds are [start, end), but range(start, end - 1) excludes index end - 1. A one-row page therefore returns no rows, and each full page loses its last row; render_page and summarize expose that truncated output.

findings.title: Return cache entries only while they are still fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed comparison returns a value only after its age exceeds ttlMs; a newly stored entry is deleted and returned as null, while expired entries remain readable indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove every completed job when pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the current index, then forEach advances past it. For example, `[done, done, pending]` returns `[done, pending]`, leaving a completed job queued.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time near zero, so it fails `elapsed > ttlMs`, is deleted, and `get` returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item left while `forEach` advances its index. For `[done, done]`, the second job is skipped and returned despite being completed.

findings.title: Return cache entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, so it fails the `> ttlMs` check, is deleted, and `get` returns null. Entries older than the TTL are instead returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while forward-iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: For `[doneA, doneB, pending]`, removing `doneA` shifts `doneB` to index 0 while `forEach` advances to index 1; it then examines `pending`, leaving `doneB` in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [100, 20, 3], rankScores returns [3, 20, 100], so topPlayers(..., 1) uses 3 as the cutoff and returns the first input player rather than the 100-point player. formatBoard exposes the incorrect ranking.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before computing the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Default Array.sort compares values as strings. With scores [9, 80, 70] and n=2, rankScores returns [9, 80, 70], so topPlayers uses 80 as the cutoff and omits the legitimate second-highest score, 70.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort without a comparator sorts scores as strings. For [{name:'low',score:9},{name:'high',score:100}] with n=1, rankScores produces [9,100], sets cutoff to 9, and topPlayers returns the first input player ('low') instead of the 100-point player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed comparison uses `==` for an attacker-controlled signature. This may return after the first differing character, revealing partial HMAC matches through timing; `hmac.compare_digest` is intended to avoid that leak.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `==` comparison may reveal how much of the HMAC matches through timing. A successful `verify` result directly authorizes `processor(payload)` in `app/webhook.py:14`.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `==` comparison can short-circuit on a mismatched signature prefix, exposing a timing oracle to attackers able to submit repeated webhook requests. This verification directly controls whether `processor(payload)` executes.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the context at line 22 exits. If either subsequent balance UPDATE fails, the function raises after a committed ledger entry; if the debit succeeds and the credit fails, balances can also be left partially applied. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits after `_record_ledger` and before either balance update runs. If a balance update fails, the ledger entry remains committed; if the destination update fails after the debit succeeds, account balances can become one-sided. Previously, all three writes were within the same transaction.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line runs both balance updates after the transaction has committed the ledger insert. If either update fails, the ledger entry remains durable; if the credit update fails, the debit may also remain applied without a corresponding credit.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The local-time getters assign the same instant to different billing days depending on the process timezone. For example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 on an America/Los_Angeles host, while the prior implementation returned 2026-01-01.

findings.title: Keep billing-day partitioning in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return statement replaces UTC getters with local-time getters. The same instant therefore falls into different billing-day buckets on different hosts; for example, 2026-08-04T20:00:00Z is 2026-08-05 in UTC+08. This changes emitted billing-day values based on deployment timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing-day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed local-time getters make the same instant produce different billing keys on hosts in different timezones; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A/account X populates `memo`, tenant B/account X returns the cached tenant A Profile at the early return instead of invoking its tenant-specific `fetchProfile`.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A loads account X, memo stores tenant A's Profile under `X`. A later `readProfile(tenantB, X, ...)` returns that cached profile at line 16 without calling `fetchProfile`, exposing the wrong tenant's profile.

findings.title: Include tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants with the same account ID now share one memo entry. After tenant A loads account X, a read for tenant B/account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing the wrong tenant's profile data.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed catch converts the missing-key Error into "", making a failed lookup indistinguishable from a stored empty string. The exported load API therefore reports failure as successful data; src/store.ts:12 then includes that fallback in loadAll results.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: `load` is exported and previously threw on an absent key; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a stored empty string. `loadAll` at `src/store.ts:12` therefore returns partial-looking data instead of signaling a missing required key.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A Map<string, string> can legitimately contain "", so a missing key is now indistinguishable from a present key whose value is empty. loadAll propagates that fallback at src/store.ts:12, causing callers to receive apparently valid values instead of the prior missing-key error.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry Config callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Config used by retry replaces timeoutMs with timeout and newly requires retries. Existing TypeScript callers using { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check. JavaScript callers retaining timeoutMs cause Date.now() + undefined to become NaN, so the deadline check never expires.

findings.title: Expose permanent background retry failure
findings.whyItBreaks: When every fn invocation throws, retryBackground catches every error and returns void after exhaustion. This is identical to its success result, so public callers cannot distinguish permanent failure from successful completion.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers constructing the formerly valid `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` config can no longer compile: `timeoutMs` was removed, `timeout` is now required, and unrelated `retries` is also required even when calling the unchanged `retry` API.

findings.title: Signal exhausted background retries to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: When every callback attempt throws, this exported function exits with the same `void` result as a successful callback. Callers cannot distinguish a completed background operation from one that never succeeded.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers of exported retry() that pass { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer satisfy Config because timeoutMs was removed and retries and timeout are newly required. JavaScript callers that still pass timeoutMs produce a NaN deadline, so retry() ignores its timeout.

findings.title: Expose failure after retryBackground exhausts retries
findings.whyItBreaks: When every invocation throws, retryBackground returns void exactly as it does after a successful invocation. As an exported API, this forces callers to conflate retry exhaustion with success.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now permits `number`, but the changed rendering logic reads `value.length`; numbers have no `length`, so `<Field value={42} />` yields `len=undefined` and fails type checking.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts `number`, but `value.length` is invalid for that union. A valid numeric prop therefore fails type-checking and would produce `len=undefined` if executed without type checking.

findings.title: Support numeric Field values before widening the prop type
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop contract accepts numbers, but the changed implementation reads `value.length`; a number has no `length`, so `<Field value={42} />` produces `len=undefined` at runtime.

findings.title: Preserve the larger buffer for diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` returns the complete patch through this helper. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node's 1 MiB default; a PR diff above that limit now causes the adapter to throw before it can submit any review. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these PRs.

findings.title: Retain the git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff` can exceed Node's default 1 MiB `spawnSync` buffer. Without the previous 64 MiB limit, the command fails before `review(bundle)` is called, so no review is posted.

findings.title: Keep baseSha aligned with the patch base
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and changed-file set are computed from `mergeBase` (lines 140-141), while the bundle now reports `baseSha`. If the PR target branch advanced after the branch forked, `baseSha..headSha` describes a different diff from the supplied patch.

findings.title: Keep the bundle base SHA aligned with the generated patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and changed-file list are calculated from mergeBase (lines 140-141), but the bundle now reports baseSha, the current PR target SHA. If the target branch advanced after the PR branch diverged, consumers using bundle.baseSha..headSha inspect unrelated target-branch commits while the supplied patch describes only mergeBase..headSha.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for review patches
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. A valid PR whose git diff output exceeds that size makes spawnSync fail, so the review check fails before it can review the PR.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` means the subprocess no longer explicitly prevents the review agent from writing in `opts.repoPath`. Because `spawnSync` runs Codex with that repository as its working directory, a write-capable configuration can alter the repository under review.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes the Codex subprocess inherit its configured/default sandbox while running with `cwd: opts.repoPath`. A review prompt can therefore modify the repository being reviewed, invalidating the review and potentially changing user files.

findings.title: Keep the Codex invocation read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` delegates sandbox policy to the external Codex configuration/default while Codex runs in `opts.repoPath`. It can therefore modify the checkout being reviewed, removing the wrapper's prior containment.

findings.title: Compute the PR patch from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA can be a base-branch tip that advanced beyond the PR fork point. Diffing that commit directly against HEAD includes base-only changes, so the review bundle and inline-comment path can analyze files not changed by the PR.

findings.title: Use the configured PR head for the review diff
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_HEAD_SHA still identifies the commit in the Bundle and is used when posting the review, but the patch is now read from the checkout's HEAD. When Actions checks out a merge ref or another revision, Needlefish reviews that revision while posting the result to PR_HEAD_SHA, producing incorrect review content and potentially invalid inline comments.

findings.title: Generate the review range from the PR head and merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed lines generate `patch` and `changedFiles` from `baseSha` to the checkout's `HEAD`, while the bundle and published review still use `headSha` from `PR_HEAD_SHA`. If the checkout is a synthetic PR merge commit, its diff can include changes not present on the PR head, so the review attached to `headSha` can describe a different range. Restore the merge base of `baseSha` and `headSha`, and diff it to `headSha`.

findings.title: Use the supplied PR head SHA for review inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA identifies the PR commit but the checkout is a synthetic merge commit, the patch and changed-file set are built against HEAD rather than headSha. The review can therefore describe different content from the commit_id submitted to GitHub.

findings.title: Preserve prompt data as literal replacement text
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed string replacements interpret `$&`, `$`` and `$'` in the replacement text. A patch or serialized finding containing one of these tokens is altered before `runCodex` receives the prompt, so the review or critic operates on corrupted input.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets `$&`, `$`` and `$'` in string replacements. A valid patch, bundle, or candidate finding containing these sequences is transformed before being passed to Codex, producing corrupted review input.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads when replacing placeholders
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed String.replace calls treat `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in bundle.patch, bundle JSON, or candidate JSON as replacement tokens. A patch containing `$&`, for example, inserts the placeholder match instead of the literal patch text, so the review or critic prompt can be corrupted and produce an incorrect verdict.

findings.title: Preserve commit_id in the fallback review request
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary request analyzes and targets headSha, but the changed fallback omits commit_id. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the PR's latest commit, so a push between analysis and a failed inline-comment POST can attach findings for the older SHA to the newer commit.

findings.title: Pin the fallback review to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review POST fails, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub defaults such a review to the PR's current latest commit, while this run's result was computed for headSha. A push between the two requests can therefore attach a stale review to the newer commit.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or incomplete findings are converted into actionable-looking Finding objects: an invalid severity becomes P1, while missing file and line data become an empty path and line 0. normalizeReview emits these fabricated entries rather than reporting malformed review output, so callers cannot distinguish invalid model output from a genuine finding.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-finding errors
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported and now maps findings through a normalizer that replaces invalid severity/category and missing required fields with defaults. For example, severity "P9" becomes "P1" and a missing file becomes "", so consumers receive a seemingly valid Finding instead of a detectable validation failure.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severity/category and missing file or line fields now become a P1/bug finding with file="" and lineStart=0 rather than an error. The returned Finding carries no invalid marker, so consumers receive malformed review output as a real finding.

findings.title: Retain strict=false behavior for existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously exported a strict=false mode that discarded malformed findings. Removing the parameter breaks TypeScript callers that pass it; JavaScript callers silently switch from dropping invalid entries to returning defaulted findings.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so lines 38-39 run before the first checkout at lines 42-46. Removing --repo leaves gh pr view without a repository supplied by this workflow; on a clean self-hosted runner it has no checkout/remote to infer from, while a reused runner can inherit stale repository context. Manual dispatches can therefore fail to resolve the requested PR or resolve one from the wrong repository.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit for manual PR ref resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and this step runs before actions/checkout. Without -R "$REPO", `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` has no guaranteed repository context and fails instead of emitting head/base SHAs, so manual review runs cannot proceed.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository when resolving dispatched PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and these commands run before the first actions/checkout step. Without -R, gh pr view must infer a repository from the current directory's git remote, but no repository has been checked out. The manual review workflow therefore fails before it can resolve or check out the requested PR.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer now converts null and missing or incorrectly typed required review fields into an empty RawReview. Consumers can no longer distinguish malformed model output from a legitimate empty review.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer no longer rejects a non-object payload or a payload missing required review fields. Instead, it returns a valid RawReview with an empty summary and arrays, so consumers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a legitimate empty review.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer now turns a non-object or payload missing required top-level fields into a valid-looking empty review. A malformed response is therefore indistinguishable from a genuine clean review, so callers can persist or report invalid output as a pass-like result.

findings.title: Resolve PR refs for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so line 29 falls back to github.ref—the branch selected to run the workflow, rather than the PR selected by pr_number. The reviewer consequently runs against that branch, while lines 45-46 pass empty PR SHA values to its invoked CLI at line 47.

findings.title: Resolve PR refs before manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, the pull_request fields are empty. The changed checkout falls back to github.ref (the branch selected for dispatch), BASE_REF falls back to main, and both SHA environment variables are empty. Dispatching from main to review PR #123 therefore checks out main rather than the PR head; non-main PR bases are also fetched incorrectly.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore falls back to github.ref, while PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are empty. The required pr_number no longer determines the checked-out code or diff, so manually triggered reviews cannot reliably review the selected PR.

findings.title: Restore a sufficient stdout buffer for git diff
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the complete patch through `git diff` at line 100. With `maxBuffer` removed, Node's default 1 MiB buffer applies; a larger diff makes `spawnSync` fail, and the status guard throws instead of producing a review. The prior implementation explicitly supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Preserve the enlarged buffer for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `spawnSync` options at line 11 omit `maxBuffer`, restoring Node's 1 MiB default. `runLocal` obtains the complete review patch with `git diff` at src/adapters/local.ts:100, so diffs exceeding that limit fail before a review can be submitted.

findings.title: Restore the git diff buffer allowance
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the entire patch through `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])`. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses its 1 MiB default and terminates oversized diff output; the resulting nonzero/null status causes `git()` to throw, so local review cannot process otherwise valid larger PRs. The previous implementation explicitly supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The error path now publishes a completed check with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". Neutral is accepted as a successful check conclusion, so a required Needlefish check can permit merging even though review() threw and no review verdict was produced.

findings.title: Bind gh pr diff to the target repository
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly added gh pr diff call supplies neither --repo nor cwd, while the surrounding PR metadata is explicitly fetched from GITHUB_REPOSITORY and changed files are computed using cwd. If the process current/default gh repository differs from cwd's repository, this can retrieve a patch for another repository's PR number or fail, so the review bundle is internally inconsistent.

findings.title: Report review errors as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path publishes the Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral" after review or posting fails. GitHub treats neutral checks as passing for required-check evaluation, so a required Needlefish check can be satisfied even though the review errored.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When review execution throws, this posts the required Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats neutral required checks as successful, so a PR can satisfy branch protection even though the review did not run; the title explicitly says it did not pass.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout independent of the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow now checks out the same-repository PR head and then runs its install lifecycle and `src/cli.ts` while exposing a token with `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`. A PR author can alter the CLI or install hooks to make authenticated GitHub API calls and forge its review state. The prior workflow checked out the review target separately and ran the reviewer from `frankekn/needlefish@main`.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the same-repository PR head, installs its dependency metadata, and then executes its src/cli.ts while GH_TOKEN has pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions on a self-hosted runner. A PR can alter the reviewer or install path to forge review output or run arbitrary code with that token.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed checkout places the PR head at the workspace root, but this HEAD contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json. The install command therefore has no package manifest or lockfile, and the review command has no src/cli.ts, so every run fails before producing a review.

findings.title: Do not execute PR-controlled reviewer code with write token
findings.whyItBreaks: For same-repository PRs, the changed steps install dependencies and execute src/cli.ts from the PR head while the job has pull-requests: write and checks: write and passes GH_TOKEN to the process. A PR can alter lifecycle scripts or the CLI to use that token to modify PR or check results.

findings.title: Canonicalize severity before validating it
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw input and maps every finding through normalizeFinding (src/shared/schema.ts:132). A valid severity such as "p0" or " P1 " now fails exact membership and is converted to P3, downgrading the emitted finding; the previous code trimmed and uppercased before validation.

findings.title: Preserve normalization of valid severity strings
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` maps untyped parsed findings directly through this exported normalizer. Values such as `" p1 "` or `"p2"` were previously canonicalized to `P1`/`P2`; the new exact-membership check returns `P3` instead, silently changing the emitted severity.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed exact-membership check rejects values such as " p0 " and "p1" that the prior exported normalizer canonicalized. Those supplied severities now become P3, silently downgrading critical findings.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit environment object makes spawnSync inherit GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. This passes deployment credentials into the Codex process and any shell commands it launches while processing the supplied prompt/repository.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the `env` option makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The spawned Codex process receives the supplied prompt, so those credentials can be exposed through prompt-directed tooling or output.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the sanitized `env` causes `spawnSync` to inherit `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. `runCodex` supplies its caller-provided prompt to the Codex process, which operates on the reviewed repository; repository-controlled prompt injection can therefore read or use the caller's GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level fork guard allows fork PRs to run on the self-hosted runner. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled PR SHA at lines 20-24, installs its dependencies at line 28, and executes its TypeScript at line 34.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed condition restricted this self-hosted job to same-repository PRs. Fork PRs now check out their head SHA and execute PR-controlled dependency installation and `src/cli.ts` on the self-hosted runner.

findings.title: Keep fork PRs off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing this job condition allows fork-origin pull requests to run on the self-hosted runner. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled commit, installs its dependencies, and directly executes its `src/cli.ts`, allowing arbitrary code execution in the runner environment.

findings.title: Preserve zero-delay runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing deployments using NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 to SIGKILL immediately now receive the 5000ms fallback; likewise NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits the 2000ms fallback before finishing. Both were accepted before this change, so this is a configuration compatibility regression that extends timed-out runner handling.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner delays
findings.whyItBreaks: A value of `0` was accepted before this change but now falls back to 5000 ms or 2000 ms. That changes timeout handling for deployments configured to skip either wait, delaying SIGKILL or final result completion.

findings.title: Preserve zero as a valid runner delay
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `parsed > 0` guard rejects an explicitly configured value of 0 and returns the fallback instead. Consequently, `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` delays SIGKILL by 5000 ms, and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` delays forced completion by 2000 ms, rather than proceeding immediately.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed code replaces each deep pass's residual risks with an empty array before passing the merged candidate to the critic. A deep pass that reports blocking uncertainty therefore cannot communicate it to the final critic/verdict result.

findings.title: Review every changed file after hotspot cap
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed code retains only six hotspots and removes the tail hotspot that covered changed files outside those selected surfaces. Such files now receive neither a deep review nor an incomplete-review signal.

findings.title: Restore coverage for changed files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews now process only the first six mapper-provided hotspots. Changed files absent from those hotspots are never sent to the deep reviewer, so defects in them can be reported as a clean review with no indication that they were skipped.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep review passes
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep review can emit blocking residual risks, but candidateMerged now replaces all of them with []. The critic therefore receives the same input for “no residual risk” and “a deep pass could not establish a verdict,” allowing an unsupported PASS to be returned.

findings.title: Keep deep-pass failures as blocking review results
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed Codex response for any one hotspot now rejects the entire large review. Previously the remaining hotspots were reviewed and the failed scope was returned as a blocking residual risk, so callers could distinguish an incomplete review from a transport/runtime failure.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Large bundles are capped at six mapper-selected hotspots, and the removed tail hotspot was the only path that deep-reviewed changed files omitted by those hotspots. Those files now produce neither findings nor a residual risk, so a review can report success while never inspecting part of the submitted change.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep review can return residual_risks, but the merged candidate now replaces all of them with []. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed large PR from one with unresolved blocking evidence, and may return a non-blocking verdict for the latter.

findings.title: Preserve focus in the large-review pipeline
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed large-review path no longer serializes bundle.focus into the map prompt and no longer substitutes it into each deep-review prompt. Since review() dispatches large bundles to reviewLarge, a caller-provided focus directive is silently ignored for those reviews while small reviews still serialize the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve focus when constructing large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Large-review prompts no longer receive bundle.focus: it is omitted from the map bundle and no longer substituted into each deep prompt. A focused request can therefore be ignored for large PRs, despite being included in the full bundle used by small reviews.

findings.title: Preserve focus and depth controls for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path no longer passes Bundle.focus or Bundle.deep to the map pass, and no longer substitutes focus into each deep-review prompt. Consequently, a caller requesting focused or deep handling for a review above the large-review threshold receives the generic large-review flow instead.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 59,500ms, `minutes` is computed as 0 while `seconds` rounds to 60, yielding `60s` instead of `1m 0s`. For 119,500ms it yields `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. These values are rendered in review call and total-duration output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, this computes minutes=1 and seconds=60, rendering `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. At 59500ms it renders `60s` instead of `1m 0s`.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: At 59,500 ms, the changed calculation produces `60s`; at 119,500 ms it produces `1m 60s`. Duration output is rendered in the Markdown result for both calls and totals. Round total seconds before deriving minutes and the remaining seconds.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger and its error text promise a positive integer, but the changed condition accepts "0" and returns 0. External callers can therefore receive an invalid non-positive value while relying on the exported parser's validation contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard accepts "0" and returns 0, although this exported function and its thrown error promise a positive integer. External callers can receive a value outside that validation contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function and its error text promise a positive integer, but changing `<= 0` to `< 0` makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` return 0. Public callers can therefore receive a value outside the documented contract.
